newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Africa mining exploration spending likely to soar.
newsitem.headline: Africa mining exploration spending likely to soar.

text.p: Africa could become the third largest destination for mining exploration expenditure as foreign companies continued to probe the continent's mineral riches, a senior mining industry official said on Tuesday.

JCI Ltd's general manager of geology Frank Gregory told delegates to a mining investment conference that spending on exploration in Africa increased by 60 percent from $199 million in 1994 to $320 million last year.
Gregory said the growth was the largest of any regional exploration budget in the world.
"Given this trend, exploration expenditure in Africa could overtake Canada in 1996, placing this continent third after Latin America and Australia," Gregory said.
He said indications were that the increase in exploration spending was sustainable.
"In 1995, there were some 23 companies committing more than $1 million per annum into exploration," Gregory said.
Mining in Africa had become a viable option in recent years by several factors, the most important being the change in attitude of many African governments toward foreign investment.

"Secondly, Africa as a result of its isolationist policies and instability, remains hugely under-explored. Application of modern geological techniques and interpretation have yet to make their impact," Gregory said.
Another reason for the expansion of the mining drive into Africa was global expectations of a new acceleration in metals consumption as emerging countries moved towards industrialisation.
Gregory said South African mining companies -- freed from the restrictions of apartheid -- were now becoming major players in the drive into Africa.
South Africa's Anglo American Corp has said it will be spending 218 million rand on African exploration in the 1996/97 financial year.
Other South African mining houses had also joined the new African exploration drive.
But Gregory said African exploration was still hampered by inadequate infrastructure, health and safety hazards, inefficient administration and corruption.
He said direct foreign investment through the private sector remained the only solution for African economies to grow and develop.
Citing the investment of junior Canadian mining companies into exploration in Africa -- C$100 million in the 1993/1994 fiscal year -- Gregory said major mining houses could soon follow.
"It is generally the juniors who blaze the trial for the larger corporate entities, notwithstanding many of the deterring factors which confront investors in Africa".
